Read-only view over a null-terminated byte string that keeps the pointer and its length. Stores the pointer the caller supplies and copies neither the characters nor the terminator, so the viewed string has to outlive the view. Null-termination is part of the contract, unlike std::string_view: the pointer stays valid input for a C interface, and the length needs no second scan.

Null-terminated: every viewed string ends in a null character, so its pointer reaches a C interface unchanged. Length fixed at construction: the view stores the length once, scanned for by the pointer constructor or taken from size() of a toy::StringLike source. Constexpr support: every operation evaluates in a constant expression. No allocation: the view holds a pointer and a length, and owns no characters. Range access: forward and reverse iterator pairs, so a range-based for and the standard algorithms read the view. Search set: substring, character, and character-set searches in both directions, each matching the std::string_view contract. Ordered comparison: equality and a three-way order over the bytes, against another view or a null-terminated byte string. Type safety: construction from nullptr is deleted, so the null case fails to compile. Exception safety: no operation throws; exceptions are off in the build.

#include "core.hpp" constexpr toy::StringView name("player"); constexpr toy::StringView alias(name); size_t letters = 0; for (const char character : alias) { letters += static_cast<size_t>(character != ' '); } const char last = *name.rbegin(); constexpr toy::StringView path("assets/player.png"); const size_t extension = path.rfind('.'); const bool named = path.contains(name); const bool isPlayer = name == "player";

Construction from a pointer: O(n) in the length of the string, one scan for the terminator. Construction from a string-like source: O(1); takes the length from size() of the source. Default construction and copying: O(1). Iterator access: O(1); each iterator is a pointer into the viewed string, or a reverse adaptor over one. Substring search: O(n * m) in the length of the view and the length of the needle; nothing is indexed or cached between calls. Character-set search: O(n + m) in the length of the view and the size of the set; each call builds one membership table, 256 bytes on the stack. Comparison: O(n) in the shorter of the two lengths; equality stops on a length mismatch before reading a character. UTF-8 character count: O(n) in the length of the view, one pass over its bytes; nothing is cached between calls. Memory usage: one pointer and one length, 16 bytes on a 64-bit target and 8 bytes on a 32-bit one.

Contracts: null pointers, offsets, and counts are checked by assert_message in debug builds, and utf8_size() validates the bytes it counts. Every postcondition assumes the preconditions of its member held. A shipping build skips the checks: a null pointer makes an empty view, an offset past the end selects an empty range, and an element access past the characters reads outside them; each member states which. Lifetime: the characters belong to whoever created them; the view neither owns them nor extends their lifetime. Type safety: the deleted nullptr_t constructor rejects a literal nullptr during compilation. Iterator validity: an iterator stays valid while the string it points into lives. Assigning to the view repoints the view alone and leaves an outstanding iterator on the previous string. Exception safety: no operation throws; exceptions are off in the build.

No operation allocates or calls into the platform, so the type suits embedded and retro targets. info The length counts bytes, not characters; under a multi-byte encoding the two differ. info A default-constructed view holds a null pointer, not a pointer to an empty string. warning A view built over a temporary dangles as soon as that temporary dies at the end of the full expression. Color with four 8-bit channels, stored in memory as R, G, B, A on every target. An array copies as is into a texture or vertex buffer whose format stores 8-bit channels in the same order; any other channel order or width needs a conversion first. The channels hold the values as given; the resource format decides whether they read as linear or sRGB-encoded.

Fixed layout: bytes R, G, B, A at offsets 0 to 3 on little- and big-endian CPUs alike. Aggregate: designated initializers name each channel at the call site. Trivial: an array of pixels or vertices is not zeroed on construction and copies as bytes. Constexpr support: construction and comparison evaluate in a constant expression.

Construction: O(1); Color32{} writes four zero bytes, a declaration without braces writes nothing. Comparison: O(1); the 4-byte alignment lets the compiler compare one 32-bit word. Memory usage: 4 bytes, aligned to 4.

Initialization: a declaration without braces leaves the channels indeterminate, as for int. Memory safety: holds no pointer and allocates nothing. Exception safety: No operation throws; exceptions are off in the build. info A vertex format places a toy::video::Color32 only at an offset that is a multiple of 4. The concept checks only the two standard concepts and the shape of those eight members. The guarantees below belong to the storage type, and a type that breaks them still compiles: A default-constructed storage has a size() of 0 and '\0' at data()[0]. Neither data() overload returns nullptr, and both point at the same bytes. The character at index size() is '\0', and size() never exceeds capacity(). setSize() takes a length no greater than capacity() over every storage, records it, writes that terminator, and touches no other character; a caller that needs more room asks reserve() first. reserve() answers true only when a following setSize() of that length is within contract, and a false one leaves the storage as it was. data() points at capacity() + 1 writable bytes, so a caller may write characters up to capacity() before it calls setSize(). A true reserve() keeps the first size() characters, moving them along when it grows the buffer. reserve() of a length no greater than capacity() keeps the buffer where it is, so a pointer into the characters stays valid across the call. max_size() never changes and is never less than capacity(), and reserve() refuses any length above it. shrink_to_fit() keeps the first size() characters and leaves capacity() no less than size(); it may move the buffer, so a pointer into the characters must be taken again after the call. A moved-from storage still meets every guarantee in this list; which characters it holds belongs to the type.

Severity scale of log calls and the macro that trims it at build time. Defines toy::log::Level, the scale every log call carries, and LOG_MAX_LEVEL, the number a call's level must not exceed to reach the binary. info Included by core.hpp only; do not include this file directly. Enumerations​ Level​ enum class toy::log::Level : int8_t strong Severity of a log message, ordered by verbosity. Enumeration values Off Nothing passes (= 0) Error Failed operation; execution may continue (= 10) Warn Condition the engine recovered from (= 20) Info Milestone of normal operation: subsystem start, asset load (= 30) Debug Coarse diagnostic detail, read while developing the engine (= 40) Trace Finer detail than toy::log::Level::Debug, down to a single call or frame (= 50) toy::log::Level::Off admits nothing, toy::log::Level::Trace admits everything, and the values between them grow with detail. A message passes a ceiling when the number behind its level is at most that ceiling. Steps of ten leave room for a severity between two neighbors. The values are contract wherever a level is stored or transmitted: never renumbered, never reused. info toy::log::Level::Off is a ceiling value only; no message carries it as its own severity. Implementations of toy::assertion for targets with no reporting backend of their own. Formats the failure into a fixed 4096-byte buffer and hands it to the registered toy::assertion::AssertionCallback, then answers what that handler decided. An unregistered handler answers toy::assertion::Action::Break, and a description that overruns the buffer ends in "...[TRUNCATED]". A failure raised while another is still being reported answers toy::assertion::Action::Ignore without a second report. Stack walking is absent, so the toy::assertion::StackWalkCallback passed to toy::assertion::setCallbacks() is ignored. info Selected by the platform CMake list of every target that carries no assertion backend of its own. Assertion failure reporting and the handlers that receive it. The application decides what a failed check does. setCallbacks() registers a handler that receives the failure description and answers with the toy::assertion::Action the check takes, plus a second handler that receives stack frames. Registration is valid between initialize() and deInitialize(). With no handler registered, a failed check reports nothing and stops at the check. Typical wiring, from the composition root: #include <cstdio> #include "core.hpp" namespace { toy::assertion::Action reportAssertion(const char * assertionString) noexcept { std::fputs(assertionString, stderr); return toy::assertion::Action::Break; } } // namespace int main() { toy::assertion::initialize(); toy::assertion::setCallbacks(reportAssertion, nullptr); // Run the application; in a debug build a failed check reaches reportAssertion() and then breaks. toy::assertion::deInitialize(); return 0; } info A check that must fail the build uses static_assert. Text utilities shared across the core types: character search and comparison, plus UTF-8 and UTF-16 conversion, counting, and validation. A search or comparison function reads only the characters inside the toy::span it is given: it needs no terminator after them, and a '\0' inside counts as an ordinary character. Counting and validation also take a null-terminated string and walk it to its terminator. Characters compare as bytes with no locale, so a result is identical across runs and targets. No function allocates. Search, comparison, and toy::string_utils::utf8Size() work in a constant expression; every other function is a runtime one, defined in a translation unit. A sequence or set search takes O(n * m) comparisons in the worst case, in the length of the range and of the pattern or set; the rest take O(n). Major, minor, and patch numbers of a build, with the revision it was built from. Aggregate the caller fills field by field; every member has a default, so an omitted number reads 0 and an omitted revision holds no characters. The three numbers rank the release. revision names the source of the build, a commit hash or a tag, and settles the order when the numbers match.

Aggregate initialization: no constructor, so designated initializers name the fields at the call site. Constexpr support: construction and both comparisons evaluate in a constant expression. Ordered: equality over all four fields, and a three-way order that reads the numbers first and the revision last. No allocation: three integers and a view; the revision characters belong to whoever created them. Determinism: the order consults no locale and holds across runs and targets. Exception safety: no operation throws; exceptions are off in the build.
#include "application.hpp" const toy::application::Version build{1, 4, 2, "9f3c1ab"}; constexpr toy::application::Version minimum{.major = 1, .minor = 4}; const bool supported = build >= minimum;

Construction: O(1) for the numbers; a revision built from a pointer costs one scan for the terminator. Access: O(1); every field is read directly. Equality: O(1) on the numbers, plus O(n) in the length of the revision when all three numbers match. Ordering: O(1) until the first number that differs, plus O(n) in the shorter revision when none does. Memory usage: three 32-bit numbers, then the pointer and length of the view; 32 bytes on a 64-bit target.

Lifetime: revision views characters it does not own, so the string has to outlive the version. Contracts: none of its own; revision inherits what toy::StringView checks. Memory safety: nothing allocates, and the numbers live in the object itself. Type safety: a nullptr revision meets the deleted constructor of toy::StringView and fails to compile. Exception safety: no operation throws; exceptions are off in the build. info A version built without a revision compares equal only to another one that carries none. Marks T as a bit-flag enumeration the operators in this header accept; denies every type by default. The primary template leaves enable at false, so no operator applies to an arbitrary type. A full specialization setting it to true, written by hand or through ENABLE_BITWISE_OPERATORS, opts one enumeration in. Every overload constrains on toy::BitwiseEnum, which reads this value, so an enumeration that never opted in reports an unmet requirement instead of silently converting. Template Parameters T Scoped enumeration over an unsigned underlying type other than bool, whose enumerators name single bits. The primary template accepts any type; a specialization grants operators only to a type that toy::BitwiseEnum also accepts.

Opt-in per type: One specialization enables the whole operator set for one enumeration. Any named namespace: ENABLE_BITWISE_OPERATORS makes the operators reachable by argument-dependent lookup, so call sites need no using-directive. Type safety: Operands and results keep type T; the underlying integer never reaches the call site. Membership tests: toy::hasAny() and toy::hasAll() test a mask without spelling the comparison against T{}. Constexpr support: Every operator evaluates in a constant expression. No allocation: Each operator forwards to one integer operation on the underlying type.

#include "core.hpp" namespace game { enum class Flags : unsigned { none = 0u, a = 1u, b = 2u, c = 4u }; } // namespace game ENABLE_BITWISE_OPERATORS(game, Flags) constexpr game::Flags combined = game::Flags::a | game::Flags::b; constexpr bool carriesA = hasAny(combined, game::Flags::a); constexpr bool carriesAAndC = hasAll(combined, game::Flags::a | game::Flags::c);
Trait: resolved during compilation; it holds one static constexpr member and no state. Each operator: O(1), one integer operation after inlining.

Contracts: none checked. The trait does not test whether the enumerators of T occupy disjoint bits, so overlapping values stay a logic error no diagnostic reports. Type safety: participation is a requires clause, so an enumeration without a specialization, or over a signed or bool underlying type, fails to compile at the call site. Value range: a result may hold a bit pattern no enumerator names. That is well defined, because T fixes its underlying type. A specialization written by hand adds none, so for an enumeration outside toy the call site needs using namespace toy; or a using-declaration per operator. Contracts: none on the record itself; the metadata pointer is not checked, a null one included. Memory safety: nothing allocates, and the message buffer lives inside the record. Thread safety: nothing synchronizes a write. A record no one writes after building it reads from any thread. Exception safety: no operation throws; exceptions are off in the build.

Let's discover Docusaurus in less than 5 minutes.
Get started by creating a new site. Or try Docusaurus immediately with docusaurus.new.
Node.js version 20.0 or above: When installing Node.js, you are recommended to check all checkboxes related to dependencies.

Generate a new Docusaurus site using the classic template. The classic template will automatically be added to your project after you run the command: npm init docusaurus@latest my-website classic You can type this command into Command Prompt, Powershell, Terminal, or any other integrated terminal of your code editor. The command also installs all necessary dependencies you need to run Docusaurus.

Run the development server: cd my-website npm run start The cd command changes the directory you're working with. In order to work with your newly created Docusaurus site, you'll need to navigate the terminal there. The npm run start command builds your website locally and serves it through a development server, ready for you to view at http://localhost:3000/. Open docs/intro.md (this page) and edit some lines: the site reloads automatically and displays your changes.
